koala.origins: The koala, Phascolarctos cinereus (Goldfuss 1817), is a marsupial endemic to Australia. Subspecies once included P. c. victor for Victoria, but there is no genetic evidence for them; any Inverleigh translocation origin is not well documented.
koala.size: Southern animals are the larger, longer-furred form. Victorian males average 12 kg and can weigh up to 15 kg, and females up to 11 kg, against 6.5 kg for the average Queensland male.
koala.distribution: Inverleigh, Teesdale and the Moorabool downstream from She Oaks have scarce sightings, fewer each decade since the 1980s. There are 19 records inside 5 km (1986–2021) and 33 inside 10 km (1983–2025); one estimate is 2 to 10 koalas, mostly in Inverleigh Flora Reserve.
koala.habitat: About 1% of Victoria's former grassy woodlands remain, and two-thirds of that remainder is the reserve between Inverleigh and Teesdale (about 1,050 ha). It is classed as an endangered ecological vegetation class, and koalas are seen occasionally among Manna Gum and River Red Gum.
koala.trees: In Teesdale and Bannockburn, koalas love River Red Gum and Swamp Gum by creeks and flats, and Manna Gum, Yellow Box and Yellow Gum on sandy plains; the reserve is dominated by Manna Gum and River Red Gum. Local trees used are not well documented.
koala.hangouts: Inside 5 km, records are in the Inverleigh reserve and Common, where koalas are seen occasionally. A mature male was seen in the reserve in January 2023, with scratches at Woolbrook and in the reserve, and two koalas at Bannockburn Bush on 30 October 2019.
koala.breeding: Koalas breed from August to March, with one young after a pregnancy of 33 to 35 days. The joey is in the pouch about six months, then eats the mother's pap and is weaned at about one year; Inverleigh births are not well documented.
koala.diet: They eat leaves of a few local eucalypts, a low-energy diet, about 0.5 to 1 kg a night, and may sleep for 18 to 20 hours. They are active for about four hours, usually after dark; which trees Inverleigh animals eat is not well documented.
koala.threats: Victoria's population is currently secure, but habitat loss, fragmentation, bushfire, drought, heat, dogs and vehicles are threats. Locally, 87% of mapped habitat has gone and a vehicle strike was recorded on 10 November 2021; chlamydia, mange and heat deaths here are not well documented.
koala.conservation: The EPBC Endangered listing from 12 February 2022 covers Queensland, New South Wales and the ACT only. Victoria is not on that list or the July 2026 FFG threatened list, and Inverleigh is a small, sparse population in remnant grassy woodland, not an overabundance site.

platypus.identification: A flattened brown body, wide dark-brown bill, webbed feet and flat tail, with waterproof fur dark brown to reddish-brown above and light brown, silver or cream below. Males have a venomous hind-foot spur, and swimming animals are sometimes mistaken for the water rat Hydromys chrysogaster.
platypus.size: Males are typically 400–630 mm and 800–3000 g, and can be over 60 cm. Females are typically 370–550 mm and 600–1700 g; length from bill to tail is up to 55 cm or up to 60 cm.
platypus.origins: An egg-laying monotreme (family Ornithorhynchidae, order Monotremata); echidnas are the only other living monotremes. It lives in eastern mainland Australia and Tasmania, and in almost all of Victoria except the Mallee; presence around Inverleigh is not well documented.
platypus.habitat: It lives in freshwater creeks, streams, rivers and lakes, from rainforest lowlands to cold high country, feeding in slow or fast water and preferring cobble and gravel bottoms. Burrows are in earth banks among native vegetation, trees, shrubs, logs, twigs and roots.
platypus.trees: Named tree species are not well documented. Descriptions mention native bank vegetation, roots, logs and stream shading.
platypus.diet: It feeds mainly on aquatic insect larvae such as mayflies and caddisflies, plus shrimp, worms, small fish, tadpoles, beetles, water bugs, snails, pea mussels and other molluscs. Food is found with bill sensory organs, stored in cheek pouches and ground on hard plates.
platypus.breeding: In Victoria, mating is normally August to October, and the breeding season August to November. Females lay 1–3 eggs, usually two, after a 21-day gestation; they hatch in possibly 10 days to two weeks, and young remain in the burrow for three months.
platypus.activity: Active all year, by day and night, but mostly at twilight and night, and most often seen swimming and diving at dusk. It usually feeds for 10 to 12 hours at night and rests by day in a short bank burrow.
platypus.bestViewing: Most often at dusk, and also at twilight and night; a recommended Inverleigh site is not well documented. Do not use opera-house nets in Victorian public waters, keep dogs leashed, and call (03) 8400 7300 for a sick, injured or orphaned animal.
platypus.hangouts: On the Leigh River (Waywatcurtan) at Inverleigh, the Barwon at Inverleigh, and their confluence, including the end of Park Street (2025) and the west bank beside a walking track (2023). Citizen science also recorded platypus at Inverleigh in the 2024–25 water year.
platypus.threats: Freshwater dependence may cause future decline. Reported risks include litter and rings, illegal opera-house nets, foxes, dogs, cats and dingoes, a platypus tick, fungal skin infection especially in Tasmania, and predators such as crocodiles, goannas, carpet pythons, eagles and large native fish.
platypus.conservation: Ornithorhynchus anatinus is listed Vulnerable in Victoria (extinction risk Victoria) on the June 2024 and July 2026 FFG lists and the FFG Act 1988. Not listed under the EPBC Act 1999; IUCN Near Threatened; protected in all states where it occurs.

eastern-grey-kangaroo.identification: Large hind legs and feet, a long muscular tail, and light grey to grey-brown fur, paler underneath, with a darker face and dark or black tail tip. Hopping, the head is held high and the tail curves up; often confused with the Western Grey Kangaroo.
eastern-grey-kangaroo.size: Males to 1.3 m body and 1 m tail; females to 1 m body and 0.84 m tail. Body up to 1.3 m, tail up to 1.1 m, and height up to seven feet.
eastern-grey-kangaroo.origins: It lives across eastern mainland Australia and Tasmania, from inland plains to the coast where annual rainfall is more than 250 mm, up to subalpine woodlands. Victoria has Red, Eastern Grey and Western Grey kangaroos; Inverleigh localities are not well documented.
eastern-grey-kangaroo.habitat: From semi-arid mallee scrub through woodlands, forest and some farmland with remnant vegetation, favouring denser scrubs and forests. Also grassy woodlands, parklands and golf courses.
eastern-grey-kangaroo.trees: Named food trees are not well documented. They favour grasses and eat a range of plants, including fungi in some cases, and sometimes leaves from trees and shrubs.
eastern-grey-kangaroo.diet: Herbivorous grazer preferring young green grass shoots high in protein; dry grass is hard to digest. Also eats other plants, herbs, sometimes fungi, and sometimes leaves from trees and shrubs.
eastern-grey-kangaroo.breeding: Breeding is continuous, peaking in summer, though most young are born in late autumn and early winter. Newborns weigh less than one gram, born 36 days after mating, begin to leave the pouch at about 9 months and leave permanently at around 44 weeks.
eastern-grey-kangaroo.activity: Nocturnal, mostly from dusk to dawn, and most active in the evening and at dawn. Large mobs gather to feed; they rest in shade or tall grass by day and graze from late afternoon to early morning.
eastern-grey-kangaroo.bestViewing: Late afternoon to early morning, when mobs feed in the open; an Inverleigh viewing site is not well documented. Kangaroos are protected; slow down at dawn and dusk, watch roadsides, and report injured or dead animals on (03) 8400 7300 because pouch young may survive.
eastern-grey-kangaroo.hangouts: The 1050 hectare reserve between Inverleigh and Teesdale, the Common, gazetted Inverleigh Flora Reserve in 1988, holds a large population or colony of Eastern Grey Kangaroos. Records name Inverleigh Conservation Nature Reserve, Inverleigh Flora and Fauna Reserve and Old Shelford Track.
eastern-grey-kangaroo.threats: Kangaroos and wallabies are among the species most often hit on roads, and the eastern grey is the species most often reported hit; they can travel at up to 65 km/h. Sometimes managed for population health and welfare and to protect people, property and biodiversity.
eastern-grey-kangaroo.conservation: IUCN Least Concern and protected by law, and not threatened or endangered among four abundant commercially harvested species. EPBC and FFG listing categories are not well documented.

short-beaked-echidna.identification: The only echidna species in Australia has a rounded body, sharp yellow-cream spines with black tips and fur between them, a long smooth snout, short legs and long sharp claws. The similar species is the Long-beaked Echidna, Zaglossus bruijni, of New Guinea.
short-beaked-echidna.size: Body length 30–55 cm, weight up to 2–5 kg, and spines about 5 cm.
short-beaked-echidna.origins: An egg-laying mammal in the family Tachyglossidae, order Monotremata. It lives across mainland Australia and Tasmania, also in Papua New Guinea and Indonesia, and has one of the largest ranges of any Australian mammal.
short-beaked-echidna.habitat: Uses almost all terrestrial habitats, including dry and wet forest, woodland, mallee, heath, grassland, bush, savannah, wetland, rainforest, urban areas, and arid and semi-arid country.
short-beaked-echidna.trees: Preferred trees are not well documented. They shelter in mulch piles and sometimes leave young in backyard leaf piles.
short-beaked-echidna.diet: It eats ants, termites, grubs, worms and other small invertebrates, taken with a long sticky tongue and ground on horny mouth plates.
short-beaked-echidna.breeding: Lays one egg, which hatches after about 10 days. The puggle suckles in the pouch for about two to three months, then is left in a burrow, where it suckles for another six months and is fed every four to six days.
short-beaked-echidna.activity: Nocturnal and diurnal. Often spotted at dusk, but can be seen at any time of day.
short-beaked-echidna.bestViewing: Often seen at dusk and at any time of day; a seasonal viewing site is not well documented. Dogs and vehicles are risks; if you find an injured echidna, contact a local wildlife help group and note the location in case a baby is nearby.
short-beaked-echidna.hangouts: Seen occasionally in the Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve. Records include Inverleigh Flora and Fauna Reserve (2010, about 2.3 km), Common Road (2021, about 2.5 km), and points about 3.5–4.8 km away on 4 November 2024, 14 October 2025 and 22 September 2026.
short-beaked-echidna.threats: Few natural enemies. Cars, dogs, foxes, eagles, Tasmanian devils, natural disasters and occasionally goannas may kill them; cats may take the young, and they are hunted for food in parts of Papua New Guinea.
short-beaked-echidna.conservation: Not listed on the FFG Threatened List or under the EPBC Act 1999. The IUCN Red List status is Least Concern; it is not endangered and the population trend is steady.

swamp-wallaby.identification: A small, stocky wallaby called the black wallaby, and the only species in genus Wallabia. Dark brown to black, often with rusty orange or yellow to orange-brown on the belly, chest and ear bases, a dark face often with a white stripe, and black ears.
swamp-wallaby.size: Reported size is 66–85 cm, body up to 85 cm, or 65–85 cm tall, with the tail up to 86 cm.
swamp-wallaby.origins: Family Macropodidae, native to eastern mainland Australia, including Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria and south-eastern South Australia, and introduced in New Zealand. Victoria’s most common wallaby, primarily along the east coast; Inverleigh localities are not well documented.
swamp-wallaby.habitat: Thick forest and woodland undergrowth, sandstone heath and swamps, with tall grasses and shrubs. They avoid open environments.
swamp-wallaby.trees: Named tree species are not well documented. Food plants are shrubs, ferns, grasses and leaves.
swamp-wallaby.diet: Native and introduced shrubs, grasses and ferns, including leaves of shrubs, ferns and grasses.
swamp-wallaby.breeding: Breeding occurs throughout the year, and a female can suckle two joeys of different ages. Pouch life is eight to nine months, and suckling may continue to 15 months.
swamp-wallaby.activity: Nocturnal and diurnal, more active by day than other wallabies and kangaroos, but most often spotted at dusk. Shy and usually solitary.
swamp-wallaby.bestViewing: Most often spotted at dusk; slow at dawn and dusk, and report hit animals so pouch young can be checked; call (03) 8400 7300. Season, an Inverleigh site, lights and feeding advice are not well documented.
swamp-wallaby.hangouts: Called Black-tailed Swamp Wallabies, with a smaller population than the kangaroos, and named in the Inverleigh Flora Reserve. Records also include Inverleigh Conservation Nature Reserve (2018), Inverleigh Flora and Fauna Reserve (2010 and 2016) and roughly 4 km south of Teesdale (1989, count 40).
swamp-wallaby.threats: Road strikes are the most common call. Roads cut travel routes, and pouch young may survive a strike.
swamp-wallaby.conservation: IUCN Least Concern; FFG Threatened List Not listed; EPBC Act 1999 Not listed. No Wallabia bicolor entry on the July 2026 FFG Threatened List, a June 2024 FFG name search, or the 28 August 2026 EPBC extract.

common-brushtail-possum.identification: Usually silver-grey above and white-cream below, with black markings around the eyes and nose, large pointed ears and a thick black prehensile tail. The call is a deep guttural cough.
common-brushtail-possum.size: Body up to 55 cm and tail up to 40 cm, and about the size of a cat. Weight is up to 4 kg.
common-brushtail-possum.origins: Family Phalangeridae, order Diprotodontia. Found in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania, Western Australia and the Northern Territory, and introduced to New Zealand.
common-brushtail-possum.habitat: Lives in urban areas, forests, woodlands, heath and open dry eucalypt forest, and in suburban trees and gardens. It sleeps in tree hollows or ceilings.
common-brushtail-possum.trees: Preferred food-tree species are not well documented. It uses open dry eucalypt forest and eats leaves, blossoms and fruits of native and exotic trees and shrubs.
common-brushtail-possum.diet: Eats leaves, blossoms, flowers, fruits, grass, fungi and insects, and sometimes birds’ eggs, nestling or baby birds, or rubbish. In suburbia it may eat almost anything.
common-brushtail-possum.breeding: One young is born in autumn or spring, and breeding is also recorded in March to May. Pouch time is about six months, then one to two months on the mother's back, with the den left at 7–16 months; gestation is not well documented.
common-brushtail-possum.activity: Nocturnal, and mostly active at night. By day it rests in a hollow log, branch, trunk or another dark place, including roofs.
common-brushtail-possum.bestViewing: At night in suburban gardens and parks. Do not feed, harm or relocate them off the property; release trapped brushtails on the same property within 50 m after sunset on the day of capture, and call (03) 8400 7300 for daytime animals on the ground.
common-brushtail-possum.hangouts: Records near Inverleigh include Common Road (2021), Teesdale–Inverleigh Road (2020), Inverleigh Common Flora Reserve (1988) and places about 3.8 km (25 September 2025) and 4.3 km away (9 May 2024). Possums emerge from tree hollows at night; brushtail and ringtail are not separated.
common-brushtail-possum.threats: Predators include dingoes, pythons, foxes and cats, and road trauma includes possums. Animals on the ground, in buildings or as orphaned joeys are common reasons for calls; a daytime animal on the ground is a bad sign.
common-brushtail-possum.conservation: Not listed under the FFG Threatened List or the EPBC Act 1999, and IUCN Least Concern. It is protected in Australia; the Central Australian subspecies Trichosurus vulpecula vulpecula is Endangered in the Northern Territory, not a Victorian population.

rakali.identification: Australian water rat (rakali): a large water-adapted rodent with webbed hind feet, a waterproof coat and a long white-tipped tail. Flattened head, long blunt nose, abundant whiskers, small eyes and ears; near-black, grey or brown above and white to orange below.
rakali.size: Body 231–370 mm, tail 242–345 mm, and weight 340–1275 g.
rakali.origins: A placental rodent (family Muridae, order Rodentia), found in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia, south-west and north Western Australia, and the Northern Territory. Inverleigh localities are not well documented.
rakali.habitat: It lives in permanent fresh or brackish water and is one of Australia’s two amphibious mammals, with the platypus. Burrows are on river and lake banks, usually hidden in vegetation, with a round entrance about 15 cm across.
rakali.diet: It eats large insects, crustaceans, mussels, fishes, frogs, lizards, small mammals and water birds. Prey is caught underwater and taken to a regular feeding site.
rakali.activity: Most active around sunset, and it may forage during the day, unlike many native rodents that are strictly nocturnal.
rakali.bestViewing: Viewing is around sunset, and sometimes by day; an Inverleigh site is not well documented. Opera-house nets are illegal in Victorian public waters because they can kill water rats, and hoop nets should be used for yabbying.
rakali.hangouts: Places include Inverleigh at about 0.4 km, 1.1 km, 1.6 km (December 2024) and 1.8 km, mostly January 2003, and Barwon River: Inverleigh (November 1966, 900 m uncertainty, about 1.1 km). Also about 4.9 km (2003) and Murgheboluc at about 8.2 km (2003).
rakali.threats: It was hunted for fur until protective legislation. Threats now include habitat alteration from flood mitigation and swamp drainage, predation by cats and foxes, and opera-house nets that can trap and kill platypus, turtles and water rats.
rakali.conservation: IUCN Least Concern, and populations are said to have recovered after protection. The July 2026 and June 2024 Victorian threatened lists have no entry for Hydromys chrysogaster, and an August 2026 national extract has no row for that name.

kreffts-glider.identification: Grey fur, dark stripe on the head and back, pale grey to cream underparts, tail black at the end with a white tip. Glides up to 50 m on a membrane from elbow to ankle; yip-yip call; eyes reflect pale red in a torch.
kreffts-glider.size: Body up to 20 cm, tail up to 21 cm.
kreffts-glider.origins: Krefft’s Glider, Petaurus notatus, family Petauridae, is the only one of the three species in Victoria. It is an Australian endemic from north-eastern Queensland to south-eastern South Australia, including Victoria, and was introduced to Tasmania.
kreffts-glider.habitat: It lives in open woodlands and forests and is arboreal. By day it uses leaf nests in tree hollows.
kreffts-glider.trees: No eucalypt species is named. Gums are named as food, and leaf nests in tree hollows are noted, without a tree species.
kreffts-glider.diet: It feeds on gums, nectar, pollen and invertebrates. Listed diet categories are arthropods, nectar and insects.
kreffts-glider.breeding: In Victoria, young are born between July and August. They are carried on the mother’s back until they can care for themselves.
kreffts-glider.activity: It is nocturnal and most active at night, sleeping by day in hollows. Groups of up to seven adults and young may share a nest.
kreffts-glider.bestViewing: Night is the only time stated. A viewing season or Inverleigh site is not well documented.
kreffts-glider.hangouts: Old Shelford Track near Carrah Track (1999) and Inverleigh Common Flora Reserve (1988 cage trap, 900 m uncertainty). Research-grade sightings: Inverleigh on 24 September 2026 and 25 September 2025, Teesdale on 11 March 2026 and 16 December 2023, and Bannockburn on 24 April 2023.
kreffts-glider.conservation: It is not listed on the FFG Threatened List or under the EPBC Act 1999. The IUCN Red List status is Least Concern.

common-ringtail-possum.identification: Grey to grey-brown above, with a white belly, white patches behind the eyes, rusty sides and orange-brown limbs. Its white-tipped prehensile tail is curled or coiled; it has round ears and a bird-like chirp, and is sometimes confused with the Black Rat.
common-ringtail-possum.size: Body and tail are each 300–350 mm, or each up to 38 cm. Weight is 700–1100 g and less than 1 kg: about half a cat, or a young kitten.
common-ringtail-possum.origins: Native to Australia (family Pseudocheiridae, order Diprotodontia), mainly in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia and eastern mainland Australia. Where it occurs around Inverleigh is not well documented.
common-ringtail-possum.habitat: It lives in forests, woodlands, rainforests, dense and coastal scrub and suburban gardens. Its spherical drey of grass, bark, branches and leaves sits in a tree hole, fork, dense vegetation or crown, several metres up, and it rarely enters roofs.
common-ringtail-possum.trees: Named food plants are not well documented beyond eucalyptus leaves, other native vegetation, and leaves of native and introduced plants, plus flowers and fruits. Shelter is in tree holes, forks or dense vegetation.
common-ringtail-possum.diet: At night it eats leaves of native and introduced plants, mainly eucalyptus and other native vegetation, plus flowers and fruits. It re-eats faecal pellets (caecotrophy).
common-ringtail-possum.breeding: Born April to November (autumn or winter): one to three joeys, mostly twins, five to six months in the pouch, then on the mother’s back. The male carries them while she feeds — the only possum known for this care — and gestation is not well documented.
common-ringtail-possum.activity: It is nocturnal, as are both common possums.
common-ringtail-possum.bestViewing: Often seen at night in suburban gardens. Season, Inverleigh sites and lights are not well documented; do not feed them, trapping without a permit is illegal, relocation is prohibited, and call (03) 8400 7300 for one on the ground, containing it only as directed.
common-ringtail-possum.hangouts: Nearest trace is an incidental record at Inverleigh Flora and Fauna Reserve (IFFR40), January 2002, about 4.9 km (100 m uncertainty). No iNaturalist record inside 10 km; reserve night possums are not identified to species, and Teesdale rows are about 6.7 and 9.9 km away.
common-ringtail-possum.threats: Joeys fall from the mother’s back, and a possum on the ground by day is a warning sign. Roofs are used where natural shelter is limited, and road trauma includes possums; other threats are not well documented.
common-ringtail-possum.conservation: It is IUCN Least Concern, and FFG Threatened List and EPBC Act 1999 status is given as Not listed. The July 2026 FFG list and 28 August 2026 EPBC extract had no Pseudocheirus peregrinus row; a missing row is not itself a Not listed statement.

bare-nosed-wombat.identification: Short, stocky and barrel-shaped, with a broad head, small eyes, large naked nose and coarse grey-brown to black coat. A hairless nose, coarser hair and narrower nasal bones separate it from hairy-nosed wombats; only two upper incisors keep growing, and the pouch faces backwards.
bare-nosed-wombat.size: Mainland average head-body is 985 mm (840–1150 mm) and weight 26 kg (22–39 kg). Also given are body up to 1.1 m, adult length about one metre, and weight 20–40 kg.
bare-nosed-wombat.origins: A marsupial, family Vombatidae, order Diprotodontia. Historically most of Victoria except the north-western corner, south-eastern Queensland, south-eastern South Australia, Tasmania, and now only Flinders Island among Bass Strait islands; almost disappeared from the western half of Victoria, and Inverleigh localities are not well documented.
bare-nosed-wombat.habitat: Temperate, often mountainous forest in south-eastern Australia, also dry and wet forest, woodland, coastal scrub and heath; it avoids rainforest. Burrows on slopes above creeks and gullies can be up to 30 metres long, and it feeds in grassy clearings.
bare-nosed-wombat.trees: Not a tree specialist. Foods include Tussock Grass in forest, Kangaroo Grass and Wallaby Grass in more open country, dry leaves, stalks, occasional bark, roots and sometimes mosses; named native trees are not well documented.
bare-nosed-wombat.diet: Fibrous native grasses, sedges and rushes, including Tussock Grass, Kangaroo Grass and Wallaby Grass. Occasional bark and reported fungi are also eaten.
bare-nosed-wombat.breeding: One young at any time of year, most commonly November to July; gestation probably 30 days. Pouch life 6–10 months, then 8–10 months with the mother; sexual maturity after two years, one joey every two to three years, and wild lifespan up to 11 years.
bare-nosed-wombat.activity: Mainly nocturnal in summer, and crepuscular, emerging when the air cools. It forages by day in cool or overcast weather, though daytime activity is unusual except in cooler months, and about two thirds of life is spent in the burrow.
bare-nosed-wombat.bestViewing: After sunset, in daytime on cool or overcast days. Inverleigh sites are not well documented; slow down in wombat territory, report dead wombats, a joey may be in the pouch, and for mange photograph the animal and call 03 8400 7300 rather than catching it.
bare-nosed-wombat.hangouts: Two records inside 5 km and no others inside 10 km: 15 April 2015, Hamilton Highway 2 km west of Inverleigh (5 m uncertainty), 25 September 2020 about 3.6 km (3262 m accuracy), too coarse for a paddock or burrow; sparse edge, not a warren.
bare-nosed-wombat.threats: Introduced wild dogs and foxes, vehicles, and sarcoptic mange, which can affect vision and feeding and can kill. Bare-nosed wombats are most affected; mites may survive in burrows for up to 16 days, and some eastern Victorian landholders treat them as causing fence damage.
bare-nosed-wombat.conservation: IUCN Least Concern, FFG Threatened List Not listed, and EPBC Act 1999 Not listed. The Bass Strait subspecies is not well documented.

agile-antechinus.identification: Light brown-grey body, lightly furred tail and a narrow pale ring around the eye. A small marsupial carnivore with a pointed face, small sharp teeth, and crinkled ears that are often notched.
agile-antechinus.size: Body up to 11 cm and tail up to 12 cm.
agile-antechinus.origins: Family Dasyuridae, order Dasyuromorphia, native to south-eastern mainland Australia. A finer Victorian range and Inverleigh localities are not well documented.
agile-antechinus.habitat: Leaf litter and fallen logs in forests, heath, woodlands and coastal plains, including wet forest.
agile-antechinus.trees: Named trees are not well documented. Logs on the ground are critical foraging habitat and refuges.
agile-antechinus.diet: Eats a variety of insects and small vertebrates.
agile-antechinus.breeding: Like other antechinus species, they die after breeding. Whether this is males only, and gestation, season and litter size, are not well documented.
agile-antechinus.bestViewing: Not well documented beyond nocturnal and diurnal activity. An Inverleigh viewing site is not well documented.
agile-antechinus.hangouts: One sighting on 19 December 2016 at 19 Ware Street, Teesdale VIC 3328, about 8.3 km away. A single street address, not a trapped series, and not treated as a resident population.
agile-antechinus.conservation: Antechinus agilis is not listed on the FFG Threatened List or under the EPBC Act 1999, and is Least Concern on the IUCN Red List.

swamp-rat.identification: Dark brown fur, usually lighter underneath, with dark brown feet, ears and tail. Ears do not reach the eyes when folded forward; the tail is shorter than or about equal to the head and body, unlike the Black Rat, and the feet are darker than the Bush Rat’s.
swamp-rat.size: Body up to 20 cm and tail up to 14 cm.
swamp-rat.origins: Native Australian Rattus in family Muridae, present for about 1 million years and close to the Bush Rat; the genus includes the invasive Black Rat. Found in eastern mainland Australia and Tasmania; finer Victorian or Inverleigh localities are not well documented.
swamp-rat.habitat: Coastal heath, sedgelands, dune scrub and grassland. They stay in native vegetation, avoid human habitation, and make tunnels through vegetation.
swamp-rat.trees: Named trees are not well documented. Food is mostly stems of grasses and sedges.
swamp-rat.diet: Mostly stems of grasses and sedges.
swamp-rat.breeding: Breeding season, litter size and gestation are not well documented.
swamp-rat.activity: Daily activity is not well documented.
swamp-rat.bestViewing: No viewing time is given. The only local row is a September 2025 species list with no time of day; do not handle a native rodent to identify it.
swamp-rat.hangouts: One September 2025 species list outside 5 km, about 7.3 km away (uncertainty 160 m), at Inverleigh VIC Barwon River Water Frontage Reserve, near -38.148, 143.993. It is not a captured animal, and that place name is not a walking track.
swamp-rat.threats: Frequent fires will prevent them from recolonising an area.
swamp-rat.conservation: The July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List has no mammal entry for Rattus lutreolus; a June 2024 search did not return the name. The 28 August 2026 EPBC extract has no row, and EPBC status is not well documented.

sugar-glider.identification: Petaurus breviceps is one local record, not a second studied species. The Sugar Glider was split into P. breviceps (coastal side of the Great Dividing Range), P. ariel (northern Australia) and Krefft's Glider P. notatus (eastern and northern Australia); only Krefft's Glider is in Victoria.
sugar-glider.origins: Family Petauridae. P. breviceps replaces P. notatus in coastal New South Wales and south-eastern Queensland, while Victoria is included for P. notatus; Inverleigh, on the Victorian Volcanic Plain west of the Divide, has Krefft's Glider as the credible local glider.
sugar-glider.habitat: Habitat for this name at Inverleigh is not well documented.
sugar-glider.trees: Tree species for this record are not well documented.
sugar-glider.diet: Diet for this Petaurus breviceps record is not well documented.
sugar-glider.breeding: Breeding for this record is not well documented.
sugar-glider.activity: Activity timing for this record is not well documented.
sugar-glider.bestViewing: A casual photograph labelled Sugar Glider is not an identification, and eyes reflecting pale red is an identification remark only. Local traces are one 2020 club record at Murgheboluc and one 2026 casual observation at Teesdale.
sugar-glider.hangouts: December 2020 at Murgheboluc (about 7.6 km, count 1) is named Petaurus breviceps. The only observation inside 10 km is a casual 11 March 2026 Teesdale record (about 8.1 km, accuracy 781 m), different coordinate from a same-day Krefft's Glider; no separate Inverleigh haunt.
sugar-glider.threats: Threats for this name are not well documented.
sugar-glider.conservation: The July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List has no mammal entry for Petaurus breviceps, and the EPBC extract has no row for this name. Absence of a row does not say the species is 'Not listed'.

grey-headed-flying-fox.identification: The Grey-headed Flying-fox (Pteropus poliocephalus), family Pteropodidae, is a large fruit bat, not a microbat, and one of the largest Australian bats. It has a fox-like face, grey head, orange-red neck ruff and grey-black fur, and uses sight and smell rather than echolocation.
grey-headed-flying-fox.size: Length is 23–28 cm and weight is up to 1.1 kg. Wingspan is over 1 m, also given as up to one metre.
grey-headed-flying-fox.origins: From central Queensland to Adelaide, mostly within about 300 km of the coast, including Victoria (most regions; fewer in the northwest), New South Wales, Queensland, some of the ACT and Tasmania. Bioregions include the Victorian Midlands and Victorian Volcanic Plain.
grey-headed-flying-fox.habitat: Roosts are in tall trees, often near water, in forests, woodlands, rainforests, mangroves, swamps, parks and botanic gardens. Camps may be permanent, seasonal or occasional; Victorian camps, especially urban ones such as Yarra Bend on Wurundjeri Country, are more permanently occupied.
grey-headed-flying-fox.trees: Camps use many trees rather than one species: more than 100 native trees plus introduced trees. Favourite blossom is eucalypts (gum trees), also paperbarks, grevilleas and banksias; they also eat garden figs and lilly pilly.
grey-headed-flying-fox.diet: Nectar, pollen and fruit, especially eucalypt blossom and figs, plus paperbarks, grevilleas, banksias and lilly pilly; they spit pulp and are pollinators and seed dispersers. Most foraging is within about 20 km of camp, with travel reported up to 50 km or 100 km.
grey-headed-flying-fox.breeding: Mating is in autumn (conception March and April); breeding September–January, pregnancy about six months, one pup in spring. Carried for three weeks or about a month, then left in crèches; flies at about three months and is weaned or independent at five to six months.
grey-headed-flying-fox.activity: They roost by day and leave the camp around sunset to forage at night. They are gregarious and nomadic, with partial winter migration, camps of many thousands (millions in the past), and travel averaging about 1,500 km a year.
grey-headed-flying-fox.bestViewing: Watch dusk departure from a distance; never enter a camp or handle a flying-fox. Treat every Australian bat as if it carries lyssavirus: wash bites, scratches or saliva contact for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent care; call 136 186 if one is injured.
grey-headed-flying-fox.hangouts: Local camps are not well documented: five March 2020 satellite fixes lie about 5.3–9.6 km from the centre, with no town or camp named. No iNaturalist observation is inside 10 km; Geelong camps are outside this circle and temporary camps follow food.
grey-headed-flying-fox.threats: Threats include clearing of habitat, especially winter- and spring-flowering trees, extreme heat, fruit netting, barbed wire, powerline electrocution, climate change and human–wildlife conflict. In Victoria it is illegal to net household fruit trees with mesh greater than 5 mm x 5 mm at full stretch.
grey-headed-flying-fox.conservation: Vulnerable in Victoria (July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee list) and nationally under the EPBC Act (effective 6 December 2001), following an estimated 30% decline over the previous 12 years. No approved conservation advice is recorded; the New South Wales status is also Vulnerable.

little-forest-bat.identification: You cannot reliably tell this bat from other Vespadelus on a fly-past. In the hand it is a tiny brown bat, paler underneath, with a raised forehead and white projections on the ears.
little-forest-bat.size: Body 3.4–5 cm and weight 3.5–6 g. Tail 2.7–3.5 cm, and wingspan up to 15 cm.
little-forest-bat.origins: Little Forest Bat, Vespadelus vulturnus, family Vespertilionidae, occurs in south-eastern mainland Australia and Tasmania. Its range includes the Victorian Volcanic Plain and the Victorian Midlands.
little-forest-bat.habitat: It hunts through eucalypt forest and woodland in south-eastern Australia, and enters farmland and townships at night.
little-forest-bat.trees: It roosts by day in colonies of up to 50 in tree hollows, roof cavities, old buildings or timber stacks. Particular roost trees are not well documented beyond eucalypts and old trees; some share a nest with possums.
little-forest-bat.diet: It takes small flying insects on the wing and may land on trees for large prey.
little-forest-bat.breeding: Females have one young in spring or summer and suckle it for 6–7 weeks. They may carry the baby while hunting, then leave it in the roost.
little-forest-bat.activity: It is nocturnal, hunts agilely on the wing and enters torpor when cold. It hibernates.
little-forest-bat.bestViewing: A dusk fly-out may show a very small bat; do not handle or rescue it. Australian bat lyssavirus may be carried by any bat: wash a bite or scratch for at least 15 minutes, seek medical care urgently, and call DEECA on 136 186 or Wildlife Victoria.
little-forest-bat.hangouts: 40 records inside 5 km and 45 inside 10 km, years 1983–2018, are mostly traps at Inverleigh Common Flora Reserve (also Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve). Latest rows inside 5 km are 2018; totals such as 82 and 59 are not a head count.
little-forest-bat.threats: It is still described as common, but it has declined where forest is logged or cleared, and it loses hollows and feeding grounds to forestry, agriculture and housing. The Indian Myna competes with it for hollows.
little-forest-bat.conservation: The July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List has no entry for Vespadelus vulturnus. In Victoria its conservation status is Secure, which is not an FFG category, and an EPBC status is not stated.

goulds-wattled-bat.identification: Brown fur covers the rear and underside, with a darker brown-black head and shoulders and a sharp distinction between them. Fleshy lobes sit at the corner of the mouth, and females are larger.
goulds-wattled-bat.size: Average weight is 14 g and average length is 11.5 cm.
goulds-wattled-bat.origins: Gould's wattled bat, Chalinolobus gouldii (family Vespertilionidae), occurs through Australia except Far North Queensland, including the Victorian Volcanic Plain and Victorian Midlands. It is also on Kangaroo Island and Norfolk Island, and the range does not extend onto Cape York.
goulds-wattled-bat.habitat: It uses dense and open woodlands, mallee, tall shrubland, open areas and urban areas, plus closed forest and open forest.
goulds-wattled-bat.trees: Named roost-tree species are not well documented. It roosts in hollows in old trees, sometimes ceilings or basements, in colonies of around 30.
goulds-wattled-bat.diet: It eats scarab beetles, caterpillars, crickets and moths, depending on the time of year. Mostly moths or beetles are taken below the canopy, and it sometimes eats seeds.
goulds-wattled-bat.breeding: Females often have twins, though birth time varies by location. Gestation is about 3 months, with young in November–December, attached in flight for six weeks and weaned in December–January.
goulds-wattled-bat.activity: In the north it is active all year; in the south, including Victoria, it hibernates in winter. In southern Australia that hibernation runs from May to late August or early September, with torpor in the cooler part of the range.
goulds-wattled-bat.bestViewing: Night sightings will not separate it from other small bats; two-tone fur and mouth lobes need a close view. Do not handle it: any Australian bat may carry Australian bat lyssavirus, so admire from a distance and call DEECA 136 186 or Wildlife Victoria.
goulds-wattled-bat.hangouts: There are 39 records inside 5 km and 41 inside 10 km (1983–2018), mainly at Inverleigh Common Flora Reserve, Old Shelford Road, Old Teesdale Track and the dam near Carrah Track. The latest inside 5 km is March 2018.
goulds-wattled-bat.threats: Threats are loss of roosts in tree hollows and of feeding grounds through forestry and clearing for agriculture and housing.
goulds-wattled-bat.conservation: The July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List has no mammal entry for Chalinolobus gouldii. An EPBC extract of 28 August 2026 has no row for this name; that is not a statement that it is not listed.

large-forest-bat.identification: Field criteria have yet to be determined for some Eptesicus, and females can be very difficult to distinguish from E. regulus. Males differ by a short bent penis, against the pendulous penis of E. regulus, and fur is often dark grey compared to lighter brown.
large-forest-bat.size: E. regulus forearm mostly less than 34 mm; females larger than 36 mm and males larger than 35 mm probably not it. Most male E. darlingtoni larger than 34 mm, occasionally as small as 33.5 mm; most male E. regulus less than about 33 mm.
large-forest-bat.origins: Vespadelus darlingtoni (Allen, 1933), large forest bat (Vespertilionidae; synonym Eptesicus sagittula), occurs in the ACT, NSW, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria, including the Victorian Volcanic Plain and Midlands. Above 300 m in the north; lower altitudes in the south, and sea level in Tasmania.
large-forest-bat.habitat: Forests and eucalypt forests, from subalpine woodland to alpine moors, and closed forest, open forest, woodland and montane areas.
large-forest-bat.trees: Colonies of up to 60 roost in hollows in old eucalypts in southern New South Wales and Tasmania. Smaller colonies sometimes use buildings.
large-forest-bat.diet: Eats moths, beetles, flies, bugs, lacewings, termites, ants and spiders.
large-forest-bat.activity: Seasonal activity and hibernation are not well documented. It flies, is gregarious, and is montane in the north of the range.
large-forest-bat.bestViewing: Not identifiable to species for a casual observer; admire from a distance. Any Australian bat may carry Australian bat lyssavirus: wash bite, scratch or saliva at least 15 minutes and seek urgent care even if vaccinated; injured animals, DEECA 136 186 or Wildlife Victoria.
large-forest-bat.hangouts: Thirty-six records inside 5 km and 40 inside 10 km, 1983–2002, at Inverleigh Common Flora Reserve (Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve): Old Shelford Road, Old Teesdale Track, Carrah Track dam and IFFR40. No later row or iNaturalist observation inside 10 km; not evidence it has gone.
large-forest-bat.threats: Loss of tree-hollow roosts and feeding grounds through forestry and clearing for agriculture and housing.
large-forest-bat.conservation: No mammal entry on the July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List. The 28 August 2026 EPBC extract has no row for Vespadelus darlingtoni; EPBC status is not stated.

lesser-long-eared-bat.identification: Light grey-brown above and white underneath, with very long ears joined above the forehead. Those joined ears are the field mark; it is not Gould’s Long-eared Bat (Nyctophilus gouldi).
lesser-long-eared-bat.origins: Lesser Long-eared Bat (Nyctophilus geoffroyi), family Vespertilionidae, occurs on mainland Australia and Tasmania, including Victoria. Mapped areas include the Victorian Volcanic Plain and Victorian Midlands and may not show the full range.
lesser-long-eared-bat.habitat: Forests, woodlands, mallee, farmland, towns and suburbs; it is common in suburbs. It also uses caves and shelter under bark.
lesser-long-eared-bat.trees: Big old eucalypts are named for nursery colonies. Roosts include hollows and fissures in old trees, under bark, old fairy-marten nests, occasional caves, and ceilings, hollow walls, unused roller doors and canvas awnings.
lesser-long-eared-bat.diet: It eats flying insects and insects taken from the ground, leaves or plants, catching them in mid-air and eating on the wing.
lesser-long-eared-bat.activity: It hunts near the ground and swoops around street lights, and it experiences torpor. Hibernation is not well documented.
lesser-long-eared-bat.bestViewing: Watch it swoop around street lights and keep your distance; only trained, vaccinated people should handle bats. Any bat in Australia can potentially carry Australian bat lyssavirus: wash bites, scratches or saliva contact for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical care.
lesser-long-eared-bat.hangouts: Twenty-two rows sit inside 5 km (1983–2002), with repeated trap sites in the Inverleigh Common Flora Reserve, including Old Shelford Road and Old Teesdale Track. Twenty-four rows sit inside 10 km, reaching 2018 at Bannockburn Bush Reserve; no iNaturalist observation is inside 10 km.
lesser-long-eared-bat.threats: Pesticides, cats, and loss of tree hollows and feeding grounds through forestry, agriculture, housing and land degradation. Cats often catch them.
lesser-long-eared-bat.conservation: It is absent from the July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List. Its EPBC status is not well documented.

southern-forest-bat.identification: Females can be difficult to distinguish from E. darlingtoni. In some areas the fur is a lighter brown and the head often appears flatter; accurate field identification is not possible.
southern-forest-bat.origins: Southern Forest Bat (Vespadelus regulus, Thomas, 1906) is in the family Vespertilionidae. It occurs in the Australian Capital Territory, New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania, Victoria and Western Australia, including the Victorian Volcanic Plain and Victorian Midlands.
southern-forest-bat.habitat: It uses woodland and is aerial. Detail beyond roosting and hunting is not well documented.
southern-forest-bat.trees: Tree species are not well documented. Roosts are hollows in old trees and under bark, often shared with Lesser Long-eared Bats.
southern-forest-bat.diet: It eats insects. The insect groups are not well documented.
southern-forest-bat.breeding: Maternity colonies form in spring, and females have one baby in early summer.
southern-forest-bat.activity: It hibernates in winter. It is aerial and gregarious.
southern-forest-bat.bestViewing: Do not handle; admire from a distance. Any Australian bat can potentially carry and spread Australian bat lyssavirus: wash bites, scratches or saliva exposure for at least 15 minutes, use an antiviral antiseptic, seek urgent medical care (injured bat: DEECA 136 186 or Wildlife Victoria).
southern-forest-bat.hangouts: 22 records inside 5 km and 25 inside 10 km, 1983–2002: Inverleigh Common Flora Reserve, Old Shelford Road, Old Teesdale Track, dam near Carrah Track, IFFR40. Leigh River, Teesdale is about 3.4 km and Kings Court, Teesdale about 5.3 km; no record after 2002.
southern-forest-bat.threats: Tree-hollow roosts and feeding grounds are lost through forestry and clearing for agriculture and housing.
southern-forest-bat.conservation: On the July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List, Vespadelus regulus is absent from the Threatened taxa sheet. Its EPBC status is not stated.
southern-forest-bat.size: The forearm is mostly less than 34 mm, and most males are less than about 33 mm. Females above 36 mm and males above 35 mm are probably not E. regulus.

chocolate-wattled-bat.identification: Brown fur, short rounded ears, and wattles on the lower lip and at the bases of the ears.
chocolate-wattled-bat.origins: Chocolate Wattled Bat, Chalinolobus morio (J.E. Gray, 1841), family Vespertilionidae; originally Scotophilus morio. Recorded in all states and territories, mainly southern and eastern mainland Australia and Tasmania, with scattered central Australian records, including the Victorian Volcanic Plain and Victorian Midlands.
chocolate-wattled-bat.habitat: Forests, and caves on the Nullarbor in South Australia. Also described as a cave dweller of montane and subtropical areas.
chocolate-wattled-bat.trees: Roost tree species are not well documented. It mainly uses hollows in old trees and disused birds’ nests, and also roof cavities.
chocolate-wattled-bat.diet: It feeds almost exclusively on moths, mainly small ones, taken below the canopy.
chocolate-wattled-bat.activity: In southern Australia it hibernates in winter. It flies fast, twisting and turning.
chocolate-wattled-bat.bestViewing: Admire from a distance; only trained, vaccinated people should handle bats. Any Australian bat can carry Australian bat lyssavirus: wash bites, scratches or saliva exposure for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent care; injured bats, DEECA 136 186 or Wildlife Victoria.
chocolate-wattled-bat.hangouts: Nineteen records within 5 km (1985–2002): Inverleigh Common Flora Reserve (also Nature Conservation Reserve), Old Shelford Road, Old Teesdale Track, IFFR40 and the dam near Carrah Track. Twenty-two fall within 10 km (to 2017), including 1993–1994 at Teesdale on the Leigh River (about 3.4 km).
chocolate-wattled-bat.threats: Tree-hollow roosts and feeding grounds are lost through forestry and clearing for agriculture and housing.
chocolate-wattled-bat.conservation: It is absent from the July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List. Its EPBC listing status is not well documented.

eastern-false-pipistrelle.identification: Names are Eastern Falsistrelle and Eastern False Pipistrelle. The back is uniform dark reddish-brown, the belly paler grey-brown, ears long and narrow towards the tip, and the second upper incisor of each pair is extremely small; field identification is not easy.
eastern-false-pipistrelle.origins: Falsistrellus tasmaniensis (Gould, 1858), family Vespertilionidae, originally Vespertilio tasmaniensis. South-eastern Australia, including the Victorian Volcanic Plain, coastal from southern Queensland to eastern South Australia and throughout Tasmania, with Western Australia also listed.
eastern-false-pipistrelle.habitat: Wet sclerophyll forest, woodland and higher-rainfall forest. It is a cave dweller and is migratory.
eastern-false-pipistrelle.trees: Tree species are not well documented. It uses hollows in old trees in higher-rainfall forests, and occasionally disused buildings.
eastern-false-pipistrelle.diet: Mostly beetles, and also other insects including moths and ants. It hunts high in the forest.
eastern-false-pipistrelle.breeding: Most young are born in December. Otherwise, breeding is not well documented.
eastern-false-pipistrelle.activity: Southern populations hibernate, and roosting colonies are often of one sex. Individuals may travel up to 12 km in a night; the species is gregarious and migratory.
eastern-false-pipistrelle.bestViewing: Admire from a distance; do not handle it, and only trained, vaccinated people should. Any Australian bat may carry Australian bat lyssavirus—wash bites, scratches or saliva exposure for at least 15 minutes, use an antiviral antiseptic, and seek urgent care.
eastern-false-pipistrelle.hangouts: Recorded between 1983 and 2002 at Inverleigh Common Flora Reserve, Old Shelford Road, nearby flora reserve sites and Teesdale. A 1983 'Inverleigh' point is the town centroid, and there is no iNaturalist observation inside 10 km.
eastern-false-pipistrelle.threats: Intensive forestry is a stated threat. Otherwise, threats are not well documented.
eastern-false-pipistrelle.conservation: Not listed under CITES, the EPBC Act 1999 or the FFG Threatened List. The IUCN Red List status is Vulnerable.

white-striped-free-tailed-bat.identification: Austronomus australis, the white-striped freetail-bat, is the largest of the free-tail bats. It is brown above and lighter underneath, with wide white stripes on each side; ears point forward and are wide and ribbed, and the free tail extends well beyond the membrane.
white-striped-free-tailed-bat.size: Body up to 10 cm and wingspan up to 40 cm. Forearm length is not well documented.
white-striped-free-tailed-bat.origins: Family Molossidae. It occurs on mainland Australia excluding the monsoonal tropics, including the Victorian Volcanic Plain and Victorian Midlands; Tasmania is absent from the state list.
white-striped-free-tailed-bat.habitat: It uses woodland and urban areas, plus wetland, dry forest, wet forest, mallee and grassland. Roosts are associated with old trees, loose bark, dead stumps and ceilings.
white-striped-free-tailed-bat.trees: Tree species are not well documented. Roosts include hollows in old trees, treeholes, under loose bark and dead stumps.
white-striped-free-tailed-bat.diet: It eats flying insects above the tree canopy, on the wing. It is also reported to forage on the ground.
white-striped-free-tailed-bat.activity: Commonly heard and rarely seen, except when flying quickly overhead; the high-pitched “ting-ting-ting” at 1–2 per second is audible to people. Hibernation is not well documented.
white-striped-free-tailed-bat.bestViewing: Listen for the audible “ting-ting-ting” and watch for a fast bat overhead. Do not handle: any Australian bat may carry Australian bat lyssavirus; wash bites, scratches or saliva for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent care (DEECA 136 186 or Wildlife Victoria if injured).
white-striped-free-tailed-bat.hangouts: Nearby records are only from 1999 and 2002, all inside 5 km: January and March 1999 on Old Shelford Track / Carrah Track (about 2.9 km), and a January 2002 bat trap at IFFR40 (about 4.9 km). No later record inside 10 km.
white-striped-free-tailed-bat.threats: Loss of tree hollows and feeding grounds.
white-striped-free-tailed-bat.conservation: CITES: Not listed; FFG Threatened List: Not listed; EPBC Act 1999: Not listed; IUCN Red List: Least Concern. The July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List has no mammal entry for this species.

rides-free-tailed-bat.identification: Ride's free-tailed bat, Ozimops ridei (Felten, 1964; CAVS 1938), family Molossidae, was named Tadarida loriae ridei and is also printed as Mormopterus loriae ridei Felton, 1964. It was reinstated as a full species; colour, ear, tail and forearm are not well documented.
rides-free-tailed-bat.origins: Ozimops ridei is in the family Molossidae. It is recorded from New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia and Victoria, with the type locality at Cairns, Queensland; the Victorian Volcanic Plain and Victorian Midlands are not among its listed regions.
rides-free-tailed-bat.bestViewing: Viewing is not well documented. Admire from a distance and treat every bat as if it carries Australian bat lyssavirus; only trained, vaccinated people should handle bats, and wash bites, scratches or saliva exposure for at least 15 minutes then seek urgent medical care.
rides-free-tailed-bat.hangouts: One January 1991 bat trap, count 1, is outside 5 km at Kings Court, Teesdale, about 5.3 km away, with 900 m uncertainty, and is a weak record. A Mormopterus ridei search returned 0 rows, and listed regions omit the Victorian Volcanic Plain.
rides-free-tailed-bat.conservation: Ozimops ridei and Mormopterus ridei are absent from the July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List. They have no row in the 28 August 2026 EPBC extract, so national listing is not well documented.

eastern-forest-bat.identification: No local record is identified as this small bat. A forearm longer than 33.5 mm is almost certainly E. darlingtoni, and accurate field identification is not possible for many species.
eastern-forest-bat.size: A small bat. Female forearms 30.1–32.7 mm (n=42) and male forearms 29.0–31.5 mm (n=30) are from north-eastern New South Wales, not a Victorian animal.
eastern-forest-bat.origins: Eastern Forest Bat, Vespadelus pumilus (J.E. Gray, 1841), in the family Vespertilionidae. Listed only for New South Wales and Queensland; Victoria and the Victorian Volcanic Plain are outside that range.
eastern-forest-bat.habitat: It is gregarious, subtropical and volant.
eastern-forest-bat.trees: Roosts include hollows in old eucalypts, including nursery colonies in the largest old trees, and some roost under loose bark. Mines, tunnels and buildings are also roosts; no local tree species is named.
eastern-forest-bat.diet: It eats small moths, flies and mosquitoes.
eastern-forest-bat.breeding: Breeding is not well documented beyond nursery colonies. No birth season is documented.
eastern-forest-bat.activity: Activity is not well documented beyond roosting and flight. It is volant, gregarious and subtropical.
eastern-forest-bat.bestViewing: Do not handle bats. Any Australian bat, including insect-eating microbats, can potentially carry and spread Australian bat lyssavirus; wash bites, scratches or saliva exposure for at least 15 minutes, use an antiviral antiseptic, seek urgent medical care, and only trained, vaccinated people should handle them.
eastern-forest-bat.hangouts: A January 1977 specimen by A. M. Gilmore, 2 km NW of Inverleigh, plotted at the town centroid -38.10, 144.05, is treated as a likely misidentification of another Vespadelus, not a local resident. No iNaturalist observation inside 10 km.
eastern-forest-bat.threats: Loss of tree-hollow roosts and feeding grounds through forestry and clearing for agriculture and housing. That is not evidence the species occurs in Victoria.
eastern-forest-bat.conservation: The July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List has no entry for Vespadelus pumilus. EPBC status is not well documented; no row in the 28 August 2026 extract is not a ‘Not listed’ status.

european-rabbit.identification: A small leporid with long hind legs, short front legs, long ears and side-set eyes, typically grey-brown with a pale belly. Juveniles often have a white forehead star lost at the three-month moult, and a running rabbit holds the tail up, showing a white underside.
european-rabbit.size: Adults usually weigh 0.8-2.3 kg. Newborn rabbits weigh about 35 g.
european-rabbit.origins: The origin is southern France and Spain, and domestic breeds came with early European settlement. They did not establish on the mainland until 1859, when Thomas Austin released at least 13 wild rabbits at Barwon Park near Geelong.
european-rabbit.impacts: At least 304 threatened fauna and flora species are affected by competition and land degradation by rabbits. Diet and damage at Inverleigh are not well documented; local signs are droppings, scratchings and diggings, and at Bannockburn rabbit holes near a creek.
european-rabbit.legalStatus: Feral or wild rabbits are declared established pest animals in Victoria. Under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994, landowners must take all reasonable steps to prevent their spread and, as far as possible, eradicate them on their land.
european-rabbit.hangouts: Inside 5 km there are 1454 European rabbit rows, and 2533 inside 10 km. Named localities include Inverleigh Flora and Fauna Reserve, Inverleigh, Murgheboluc, Teesdale, Bannockburn and the Barwon River Water Frontage Reserve.
european-rabbit.whatToDo: Report sightings, warrens, damage and control to FeralScan, and follow the product label. Coordinate with neighbours, bait in the summer break when other feed is scarce, rip warrens while soils are friable, fumigate reopenings in autumn and winter, and control foxes before rabbit control.

red-fox.identification: Only the red fox (Vulpes vulpes) occurs in Australia. Usually reddish-brown with big ears, a pale belly and a bushy tail (tip often white), it travels 10-15 km a night and rests in logs, burrows or dense cover.
red-fox.size: Males typically weigh 4-8 kg and females 4-6 kg.
red-fox.origins: Red foxes originated in Europe and were introduced for hunting in the mid-1850s, mostly around Melbourne. About 20 years later they were declared a pest in Victoria, and they now occur over 75 percent of Australia, strongly linked with rabbits.
red-fox.impacts: Foxes threaten at least 14 bird, 48 mammal, 12 reptile and two amphibian species and may eat about 400 g a night. Costs are about $227.5 million a year, or about $198 million in lost production (2020-21); an Inverleigh diet is not well documented.
red-fox.legalStatus: The red fox is a declared established pest under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994, and landowners must take all reasonable steps to prevent its spread and, as far as possible, eradicate it. Current bounty payment, dates and collection rules are not well documented.
red-fox.hangouts: Ten records fall inside 5 km and 19 inside 10 km, including Inverleigh NCR, Inverleigh Common near the golf course, and Inverleigh Flora and Fauna Reserve. Outer notes include Bannockburn and Bannockburn Bush; some foxScan points have no locality.
red-fox.whatToDo: Report foxes, dens, scats and damage through FeralScan, as integrated control with neighbours. Methods include baiting, canid pest ejectors, ground shooting, trapping, fencing, den fumigation and harbour removal; none works fully alone, and harbour may be used by native wildlife.

european-hare.identification: Flecked tan, black and white fur, ruddy brown or grey above and white below, and ears extend past the nose when held forward. They run with the tail down and it looks black; rabbits run with the tail up and it looks white.
european-hare.size: Adults are about 3.5-5.0 kg, and males are generally smaller than females.
european-hare.origins: They came from Europe and Central Asia, with the first wild Australian populations on Westernport Bay in 1862. By 1870 they were widespread in south-eastern Australia and now occupy about 700,000 km2, including open grassland, woodland, agricultural and urban areas in Victoria.
european-hare.impacts: They gnaw bark and chew stems of young trees and shrubs, a particular problem at revegetation sites, and also graze grasses, vegetables, lucerne and cereals. They ringbark young trees and vines, and RHDV2 can kill hares; Inverleigh damage is not well documented.
european-hare.legalStatus: European hares are declared established pest animals in Victoria under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994. Landowners must take all reasonable steps to prevent their spread and, as far as possible, eradicate them on the land.
european-hare.hangouts: Records show four moving between Inverleigh Golf Course and the nature reserve in Nov 2019, Inverleigh Common including Links track in Apr 2015, and sightings on 20 Sep 2024 and 14 Feb 2025. Two were in grassland at Teesdale Grassy Woodland Reserve in Sep 2021.
european-hare.whatToDo: Report hares and damage to FeralScan. Shooting, exclusion fencing, above-ground harbour removal and repellents are recommended together at landscape scale; do not treat a hare form as a rabbit warren, because ripping warrens will not remove hares, and check the tail, ears and size.

black-rat.identification: Usually brown or grey despite the name, with a pointed snout, large thin ears and a scaly tail longer than the head and body. Coat colour is a poor field mark; brown rats have a shorter, thicker tail and a blunter snout.
black-rat.origins: Probably introduced to Sydney with the First Fleet, it has spread through much of coastal Australia, including undisturbed coastal areas. It lives in roofs, cavity walls, trees and farm burrows; a local introduction story for Inverleigh is not well documented.
black-rat.impacts: They gnaw materials, foul food and cause household, commercial and farm damage, nesting in buildings, roof voids and ships. They eat cereals, grains, fruit and other nutritious items, including insects or meat; local predation on wildlife is not well documented.
black-rat.legalStatus: In buildings it is an introduced pest rodent and it was not named on the established-invasive-animals list. Glue traps are prohibited in Victoria, including commercial use, and a gazette category is not well documented.
black-rat.hangouts: Six records inside 5 km and 11 inside 10 km, including Inverleigh reserves and a needs_id observation at Teesdale on 21 Sep 2024. Tallies, including 10 at a '2KM N; RUBBISH TIP' string, are not a population or proof a tip is open now.
black-rat.whatToDo: Identify it before any pesticide: roof noise may be possums, and a reserve animal may be a swamp rat. Remove food and shelter, keep traps from children, pets and native animals, and do not use glue traps, which are prohibited.
black-rat.size: Body 165-205 mm, tail 185-255 mm and weight 95-340 g; another set is head and body 14-20 cm, tail about 25 cm and weight 200-300 g.

house-mouse.identification: Yellow chisel incisors, bulging eyes and large rounded ears; brownish-grey above, white to grey or pale yellow below, tail about body length. Active mainly at night; can jump at least 300 mm up and 2.5 m down and squeeze through an 8 mm gap.
house-mouse.size: Head and body 60-100 mm, tail 75-100 mm, weight 10-25 g.
house-mouse.origins: An introduced species found throughout Australia, sometimes reaching plague numbers when food, soil and moisture line up. Field breeding generally runs from early spring until late autumn, and longer in buildings or haystacks; the Inverleigh introduction date is not well documented.
house-mouse.impacts: Damage includes fouled food, chewed insulation, wiring and vehicle parts, dug-up seed and eaten seedlings. Losses up to 30 percent have been reported in maturing wheat, oats, barley, pulses, sorghum and maize; an Inverleigh plague or crop-loss study is not well documented.
house-mouse.legalStatus: An introduced pest that is not called a declared established pest, with no CaLP landowner duty stated. Zinc phosphide on sterilised wheat is Schedule 7 and needs an ACUP or commercial licence; glue traps are prohibited and unregistered products are illegal.
house-mouse.hangouts: The clearest reserve record is an Elliott trap in Mar 2018 at Inverleigh Conservation Nature Reserve, tally 11, 2.20 km. Other records are Jul 1989, roughly 4 km south of Teesdale, and Feb 2018 at Bannockburn Bush Reserve central block (tally 1, 9.25 km).
house-mouse.whatToDo: Close gaps down to 8 mm and seal seed and pet food. No glue traps or unlabelled poison; on a farm, monitor before control and act early; use registered zinc phosphide only with the required licence, and glove dead mice before burning or burying.

cat.identification: Feral cats are hard to tell from domestic cats, and the five local records do not say which coat or ownership class was seen. The usual coat is striped tabby; blotched tabby, black, ginger and grey also occur.
cat.size: Adult males are commonly 3.4-6.4 kg (average 4.5), and females 2.4-4.4 kg (average 3.2).
cat.origins: Cats, from Europe, Africa and Asia, may have reached Australia as early as the 17th century. Settlers brought them as pets in the late 18th century and released them in the 19th century to control rabbits and mice; an Inverleigh release is not well documented.
cat.impacts: In Victoria, rabbits are a major food, with mice, smaller native mammals, reptiles, birds and invertebrates common. They are implicated in the extinction of 25 native small and medium mammal species and threaten more than 100 other native species; a local diet is not well documented.
cat.legalStatus: Feral cats are declared established pest animals only on specified Crown land, from 26 July 2018, and not on private land. Farmers are not required to control them there, though they may manage cats among confined animals or near tethered animals.
cat.hangouts: Three records lie inside 5 km and five inside 10 km. The closest is a 1979 five-minute block 2.68 km from the centre, not a pin on Mount Pollock, and pet, stray or feral status is not well documented.
cat.whatToDo: There is no cat curfew: keep cats indoors at night where possible, contain a nuisance cat, desex, register, and get a permit for more than two cats in most residential areas. Phone 5220 7111 before trapping; a cat caught on private land goes to Council.

fallow-deer.identification: Fallow Deer (Dama dama), also called European Fallow Deer. Three white deer browsing 24.4 km south, and a mature female with a very pale, white-spotted coat at Anakie, 24.7 km away, are consistent with this deer.
fallow-deer.origins: Fallow deer are introduced game under the Wildlife Act 1975, not established pest animals under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994, and managers must control them in national parks. Victorian release history is not well documented; 344 records within 50 km and none within 10 km.
fallow-deer.impacts: Deer spread weeds, graze, rub trees, trample, form wallows and erode soil, and that pressure falls on native plants and wildlife. This is statewide, and the potentially threatening process listing is for Sambar, not fallow deer; no damage record names Inverleigh, Teesdale or Bannockburn.
fallow-deer.legalStatus: A 10-year section 7A Order allows private-land ground shooting of problem deer except Hog Deer, without an Authority to Control Wildlife, if the firearm meets the Order. Trapping, Hog Deer and other methods need that authority; section 28G authorises managers, Victoria Police and registered veterinarians.
fallow-deer.hangouts: No fallow deer within 10 km. Nearest records are 24.2–24.8 km south in 2019, 2020 and 2021 near Gherang Gherang and Anglesea, plus Anakie on 13 May 2020 (24.7 km north); 344 sit within 50 km, and none name Inverleigh, Teesdale, Bannockburn, Shelford or Murgheboluc.
fallow-deer.whatToDo: Do not treat deer as a pest duty like rabbits. No 10 km hangout to bait or clear, and absence is not proof none crossed; report a photo and precise place via iNaturalist or the land manager.

sambar.identification: Sambar (Rusa unicolor) is one of four deer species known in Victoria. One nearby research-grade record, not captive, has positional accuracy 250 m and no description text.
sambar.origins: Sambar are introduced deer and a target of the statewide deer control program. They are not an Inverleigh species in the records, and Victorian release history is not well documented.
sambar.impacts: Sambar are listed as a potentially threatening process under the Flora and Fauna Guarantee Act 1988 because they reduce the biodiversity of native vegetation. Deer damage includes weeds, grazing, tree rubbing, trampling, wallows and erosion, but damage at Inverleigh is not well documented.
sambar.legalStatus: Deer are not established pest animals under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994. On private land the section 7A Order allows ground shooting of problem deer except Hog Deer without Authority to Control Wildlife if the firearm meets the Order; Sambar is not excluded.
sambar.hangouts: No Sambar record is inside 5, 10, 25 or 50 km. One research-grade record at 25.14 km on 11 Dec 2017 (about -37.906, 144.197, accuracy 250 m, not captive) is outside the 25 km radius and is not an Inverleigh hangout.
sambar.whatToDo: Do not treat deer as a landowner duty. No Inverleigh or 10 km record means no hangout to clear, but absence is not proof a deer never crossed the district; photograph it and report the precise place to the land manager.

red-deer.identification: Red deer (Cervus elaphus) is one of four deer species known in Victoria. Aerial and ground shooting target it, alongside Sambar and Fallow.
red-deer.origins: Red deer are introduced game animals under the Wildlife Act 1975, not Catchment and Land Protection Act established pests. Release history is not well documented; known records are in Otway and Anglesea country, more than 25 km from Inverleigh.
red-deer.impacts: Deer impacts listed for the four species include grazing, browsing, rubbing, trampling, wallows, weeds, erosion and pressure on native wildlife. The potentially threatening process listing is for Sambar, and no red-deer locality inside 50 km names Inverleigh.
red-deer.legalStatus: Not established pests under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994. Private-land ground shooting of problem deer except Hog Deer is allowed under a section 7A Order without an Authority to Control Wildlife if the firearm complies; trapping still needs that authority.
red-deer.hangouts: No red deer records inside 5, 10 or 25 km of Inverleigh. The nearest public record is Bambra, 30.85 km away, on 8 Oct 2026; other records within 50 km are in the Otways, Lorne, Barwon Downs, Anglesea and Point Addis.
red-deer.whatToDo: Do not treat red deer like a rabbit-style duty. If seen, photograph and report the precise place to iNaturalist or the land manager; private-land ground shooting of problem deer except Hog Deer follows the section 7A Order, and trapping needs an Authority to Control Wildlife.

hog-deer.identification: Indochinese Hog Deer (Axis porcinus), also called Hog Deer, is sometimes confused with Chital (Axis axis). A Victorian field description and any local record to describe it are not well documented.
hog-deer.origins: Hog deer are one of four deer species known in Victoria. They are wildlife under the Wildlife Act 1975, not an established pest under the Catchment and Land Protection Act; release history and records near Inverleigh or within 50 km are not well documented.
hog-deer.impacts: Deer-impact notes cover deer as a group. The potentially threatening process under the Flora and Fauna Guarantee Act 1988 names Sambar, not hog deer, and a local impact record is not well documented.
hog-deer.legalStatus: Deer are not established pests under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994. Hog Deer were not declared unprotected on private land; destroying them off National Parks Act land needs an Authority to Control Wildlife, and unauthorised trapping is an offence.
hog-deer.hangouts: A Hog Deer hangout near Inverleigh is not well documented, including within 50 km. Nearest deer found are fallow deer about 24 km south, a fallow deer at Anakie about 24.7 km north, and one Sambar at 25.1 km.
hog-deer.whatToDo: If one is seen, report a photograph and the precise place through iNaturalist or the land manager. If it might be a Hog Deer, do not use the private-land unprotection order: an Authority to Control Wildlife is required, and trapping without it is an offence.

little-whip-snake.identification: Suta flagellum (little whip snake; synonym Parasuta flagellum) is a brown elapid, paler underneath. Its head is black from nose to neck, with a pale brown stripe across the top of the nose, and light brown lips, face sides and area below the eyes.
little-whip-snake.venom: The little whip snake is not thought to be highly dangerous to humans, but any snake bite must be treated with caution. Victorian elapids are venomous, and young snakes are as venomous as adults.
little-whip-snake.activeSeason: The species is mainly nocturnal. Australian snakes are most active in spring and summer; in southern Australia they brumate in winter and often come out on sunny days, so a winter encounter is possible.
little-whip-snake.habitat: Little whip snakes are found under rocks or logs, especially on stony hills close to grasslands or eucalypt woodlands, in south-eastern mainland Australia. Named local shelter notes are survey tiles around Bannockburn, which are survey shelters rather than natural habitat.
little-whip-snake.diet: Little whip snakes hunt mainly small lizards. Local prey around Inverleigh is not well documented.
little-whip-snake.breeding: Females give birth to about seven live young. Birth month, mating season, size at birth and local births are not well documented.
little-whip-snake.hangouts: Within 5 km, the only named locality is roughly 4 km S of Teesdale (6 July 1989), plus a place guess of Inverleigh (16 October 2020). Named records further out are around Bannockburn, including Harvey Rd, Lownde Bridge and Bannockburn Bush.
little-whip-snake.conservation: It is not on Victoria's Flora and Fauna Guarantee threatened list, and it has no EPBC threatened-species row. A New South Wales Vulnerable status and an ACT restricted-trade status are not Victorian categories; all native reptiles remain protected under the Wildlife Act.

lowland-copperhead.identification: The Inverleigh records are lowland copperhead, Austrelaps superbus, the south-eastern species (southern Victoria and Tasmania), not highland or pygmy copperhead. Look for a moderately robust snake, blackish to red-brown, narrow head, round pupil, barred lips and pale belly; a coppery snout is not always there.
lowland-copperhead.venom: A bite from an adult copperhead may be potentially fatal without medical assistance. Venom is powerfully neurotoxic, haemolytic and cytotoxic; they tend to avoid people, and if cornered hiss, flatten and thrash, usually without biting unless provoked further.
lowland-copperhead.activeSeason: They emerged from winter quiescence in August or September, depending on the year, and entered shelters in late April or early May. Mostly diurnal and on the ground, they also come out on warm evenings and sunny winter days, and sometimes climb to bask.
lowland-copperhead.habitat: It lives in grassland, heath, woodland and open scrub, often near swamps, creeks and rivers, and in farmland more than a century old around dams, drains and road verges. Shelter includes logs, dense vegetation and burrows; named local places are Inverleigh Common and Inverleigh Cemetery.
lowland-copperhead.diet: They feed on frogs, lizards and small mammals; copperheads as a group eat mostly skinks, also frogs, lizard eggs, snakes and occasional birds and mammals, and are cannibalistic. Prey at Inverleigh is not well documented.
lowland-copperhead.breeding: They bear live young; wild females do not breed every year. Litters of 9 to 45 (average 15) fall in January to March, and up to 30 young in mid to late summer; a March mating report's wild or captive origin is not well documented.
lowland-copperhead.hangouts: Three records sit inside 5 km: Inverleigh Cemetary, 29 April 1997, about 1.0 km west; Inverleigh Common, 8 April 1995, about 4.8 km north; and a research-grade Inverleigh sighting, 14 February 2025, about 1.4 km north-east. No other copperhead lies in the 5–10 km ring.
lowland-copperhead.conservation: The lowland copperhead was not found on the FFG Threatened List or in the EPBC extract, and is not listed as threatened. It remains protected as native wildlife.
lowland-copperhead.size: Total length is published both to 145 cm, with males larger, and up to 1.7 m.

eastern-brown-snake.identification: Slender to moderate, head barely distinct from the neck. Colour can be brown to near black, tan, chestnut or orange, belly cream, yellow or orange and may be blotched; young have a black head and sometimes bands or dark stripes that fade.
eastern-brown-snake.size: Average total length is around 1.5 m; the largest reliably measured specimen was 2013 mm, and length is also reported up to 2 m. One animal inside 5 km was about 1.8 m long.
eastern-brown-snake.venom: This species causes more deaths than any other Australian snake, and the bite is dangerously venomous and can be fatal. The initial bite is often painless, so seek medical attention without delay and do not kill the snake for identification.
eastern-brown-snake.activeSeason: Active in spring and summer, plus sunny winter days in the south. They hunt by day and, when hot, in the late afternoon; local dates are 19 October 2014, 30 October 2019 and 6 July 1989, and a local calendar is not well documented.
eastern-brown-snake.habitat: Open woodland, scrub and savannah grassland, plus grassy woodland in Inverleigh Conservation Reserve off Common Road, and also coastal heath and dry sclerophyll forest. It shelters in logs, rocks, soil cracks, burrows and iron, and is abundant at agricultural and suburban edges.
eastern-brown-snake.diet: They eat frogs, reptiles and reptile eggs, birds, and mammals, particularly introduced rats and mice, and juveniles take more lizards. They may use venom and constriction and can chase prey; local stomach contents are not well documented.
eastern-brown-snake.breeding: Lays eggs from mid to late spring, clutch averaging 15 and up to 25 and up to 35, in soil cracks or communal nests in rabbit warrens. Incubation is 36 days at 30°C and 95 days at 25°C; no local record is a nest.
eastern-brown-snake.hangouts: One inside 5 km: Inverleigh Conservation Reserve off Common Road, 19 October 2014, about 1.7 km north of the centre. Bannockburn Bush, 30 October 2019, about 8.1 km; roughly 6 km south-west of Lownde Bridge, 6 July 1989, about 9.3 km; Teesdale about 7.8 km.
