eastern-brown-snake.conservation: It is not endangered, still protected wildlife, and killing one on a farm is not legal. It uses disturbed country and eats house mice; many are killed on roads and by landowners, but local deaths are not well documented.

snake-safety-general.identification: Inside 5 km and 10 km, recorded snakes are the little whip snake, lowland copperhead and eastern brown snake. Tiger snakes and red-bellied black snakes are not recorded within 10 km; nearest are about 11.8 km (Bannockburn, November 2024) and 28.4 km (December 1989).
snake-safety-general.venom: Eastern brown snakes cause more deaths than any other Australian snake; the neurotoxic, procoagulant bite is often painless and can be fatal. Lowland copperhead bites can be fatal, while little whip snake bites are not thought highly dangerous but treated with caution.
snake-safety-general.activeSeason: Snakes are most active in spring and summer, and southern Australian snakes brumate in winter but often emerge on sunny days. In a southern Victorian study, lowland copperheads emerged about August or September and retreated in late April or early May.
snake-safety-general.habitat: Snakes use rocks, logs and leaf litter, often within a few hundred metres of water, and yards with water or mice. Long grass, rubbish and rodents bring them closer to houses; local records include Inverleigh Common, the cemetery and the conservation reserve.
snake-safety-general.diet: The little whip snake eats mainly small lizards. The lowland copperhead takes frogs, lizards and small mammals, and the eastern brown snake takes frogs, reptiles, birds and especially rats and mice, which can draw snakes into yards.
snake-safety-general.breeding: The little whip snake and lowland copperhead bear live young, while the eastern brown snake lays eggs. No birth or nest is in the Inverleigh records.
snake-safety-general.hangouts: Nearest tiger snake: Saffin Court, Bannockburn, 17 November 2024, about 11.8 km; nearest red-bellied black snake about 28.4 km away, roughly 2 km west of Fairy Park, December 1989. One white-lipped snake is about 18.3 km on the Mount Mercer–Shelford road at Shelford, April 2018.
snake-safety-general.conservation: Every native reptile is protected under the Wildlife Act 1975 whether or not it is threatened. These species were not on the July 2026 threatened list; the only related listing is Krefft's Tiger Snake (Flinders Ranges), Vulnerable, not the Victorian tiger snake.

jacky.identification: Jacky Lizard, also called Jacky Dragon, is Amphibolurus muricatus (White, 1790). It is grey to dark brown, with darker triangular patches that often form a zigzag, an orange-yellow mouth interior, and a small crest along the back of the neck.
jacky.size: Snout-to-base-of-tail length is up to 12 cm.
jacky.habitat: They live in sclerophyll forests, coastal woodlands and open woodland, forest and scrub, usually with some native vegetation. They bask on logs, fallen branches or rocks; local notes include a burrow on Old Teesdale Track and cover in Lepidosperma.
jacky.diet: They eat a wide range of small arthropods, including insects and other invertebrates. No local record names a prey animal.
jacky.activeSeason: They are active by day and are often seen basking. Records within 10 km fall in March, April, August, September, October, November and December, from 1998 to 2024.
jacky.breeding: They lay eggs. Clutch size, mating month and nest site are not well documented, and no local record is a nest or a clutch.
jacky.hangouts: Inside 10 km, records name Inverleigh Conservation Reserve, Old Shelford Track south of Teesdale, Inverleigh Common, Teesdale, Mason's Road at Bannockburn, and Bannockburn Bush Reserve.
jacky.threats: A startled animal runs into leaf litter or under trees or logs. Under the Wildlife Act 1975 it is illegal to wilfully disturb, hunt, take, trap or kill wildlife without a permit, and relocating wildlife requires an Authority to Control Wildlife.
jacky.conservation: It is not on the Flora and Fauna Guarantee Act Threatened List or the EPBC threatened-species extract, and that does not remove Wildlife Act protection. Its IUCN category is not well documented.

eastern-three-lined-skink.identification: Eastern Three-lined Skink, Acritoscincus duperreyi (Gray, 1838), occurs in Victoria, including the Victorian Volcanic Plain and the Victorian Midlands. It has a grey or metallic brown body, a wide black stripe along the side, and a throat that is often orange-red.
eastern-three-lined-skink.size: Snout-vent length is up to 6 cm, and maximum size is 10 cm.
eastern-three-lined-skink.habitat: It lives in woodlands, grasslands and heathlands, and may climb low grass tussocks or shrubs to bask. At Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve, with trees and a wallaby-grass ground layer, two animals were found under logs and metal debris on 10 March 2018.
eastern-three-lined-skink.diet: The diet is invertebrates and insects. Local prey is not well documented.
eastern-three-lined-skink.activeSeason: Inside 5 km the four rows are March (2) and October (2), 2018–2022. Inside 10 km, rows from 1989–2025 include January, March, June, July, September, October and November.
eastern-three-lined-skink.breeding: Up to three females may nest together, each laying a clutch of up to five eggs. No local record describes a nest.
eastern-three-lined-skink.hangouts: Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve (10 March 2018, two under logs and metal debris) plus Inverleigh records on 31 October 2020 and 11 October 2022. Farther out: Harvey Road paddocks at Bannockburn, a July 1989 record near Lownde Bridge, Teesdale (29 June 2025) and Bannockburn Bush.
eastern-three-lined-skink.threats: No local record describes a cat, dog, mower, snail bait or road death. Native reptiles are protected under the Wildlife Act 1975.
eastern-three-lined-skink.conservation: It does not appear on the FFG Threatened List or in the EPBC species extract, and Wildlife Act 1975 protection still applies. Its IUCN status is not well documented.

garden-skink.identification: The Pale-flecked Garden Sunskink (Lampropholis guichenoti), also called the Common Grass Skink, is a small grey-brown or olive-brown skink. It has a dark brown stripe from the neck to the tail on the back and side, often speckled, and a whitish or silvery-grey belly.
garden-skink.size: Snout-vent length is up to 6 cm, and maximum size in the field is 10 cm. One animal was about 8 cm long.
garden-skink.habitat: It is found from wet and dry sclerophyll forest to coastal and mountain heaths, and commonly in suburban gardens. It is terrestrial, using low open woodland, open forest, tall forest and woodland, and often basks or forages among leaf litter and rock piles.
garden-skink.diet: Garden skinks feed on small invertebrates. Named prey around Inverleigh is not well documented.
garden-skink.activeSeason: It is diurnal. Within 10 km the rows (1989 to 2025) include January, February, March, April, July, September, October, November and December. A July record means this file does not say the species is absent in winter.
garden-skink.breeding: The species is oviparous, and females congregate to lay up to four eggs each in communal nests that can contain more than 200 eggs. Local nests around Inverleigh and Bannockburn are not well documented.
garden-skink.hangouts: Within 5 km: a coarse place guess, Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve (about 2,515 m), and a site roughly 4 km S of Teesdale. At the Bannockburn tile-grid coordinate: 17 animals (16 October 2017), 6 (12 November 2017) and 7 (12 September 2018).
garden-skink.threats: Cited garden practice is to leave logs and rocks and keep baits away from native animals. No local row describes a cat, dog, mower, snail bait or road death, so local injury is not well documented.
garden-skink.conservation: A text search of the FFG Threatened List, July 2026, found no Lampropholis guichenoti, and the EPBC extract of 28 August 2026 does not list it. Wildlife Act 1975 protection still applies, and the IUCN status is not well documented.

eastern-blue-tongue.identification: Two local skinks, not snakes: eastern or common (Tiliqua scincoides), grey with brown or blackish bands and a black line behind the eye; blotched (Tiliqua nigrolutea), brown to black with pink, cream or yellow blotches. Short legs, a large head and a blue warning tongue.
eastern-blue-tongue.habitat: They live in open country, grassland, heath, woodland, forest and suburban gardens with low shrubs or tall grass. They shelter under logs, rocks, leaf litter or debris, bask on concrete, stone or brick, and stay mostly inactive in colder months.
eastern-blue-tongue.diet: They eat a wide mix of plants and slow-moving animals, including insects, beetles, snails, slugs, carrion, wildflowers, native fruits and berries, and crush shells with strong jaws. Local meals are not well documented; do not feed them.
eastern-blue-tongue.activeSeason: They are active by day, basking in the morning and foraging later, and stay inactive in cold weather except for sunny-day basking. Nearby records fall in January, May, September, October, November and December (1996–2020); within 5 km only January and December.
eastern-blue-tongue.breeding: Live-bearing: males pursue females from September to November, and young are born from December to April (eastern animals usually December–January). Reported litters are usually about 10 and up to 19, or up to 25; young disperse within a few days.
eastern-blue-tongue.hangouts: Within 5 km, records are Old Shelford Track (8 December 1998) and a 22 January 2015 Inverleigh sighting that names no street or reserve. Farther out: Inverleigh Common, Spring Creek Road, a Harvey Road paddock, Teesdale and Bannockburn Bush.
eastern-blue-tongue.threats: Snail bait, dogs, cats, mowing and warm roads can injure or kill them; the only local injury note is the 25 May 2017 Spring Creek Road roadkill. They are not venomous, but a frightened animal may bite if picked up.
eastern-blue-tongue.conservation: Tiliqua scincoides is not on the Victorian FFG Threatened List and has no EPBC threatened listing; the critically endangered northern subspecies is a different animal. Wildlife Act protection still applies; IUCN status is not well documented.
eastern-blue-tongue.size: Eastern blue-tongues reach almost 600 mm total (about 360 mm head and body), or up to 35 cm snout to tail base and 45 cm maximum. The blotched blue-tongue’s tail is shorter than its body.

blotched-blue-tongue.identification: Dark chocolate brown to black with large pink, cream or yellow blotches and a tail banded in those colours, without the black line behind the eye of the stripy eastern blue-tongue. Underside cream, yellow or pinkish with black mottling; limbs speckled black and white.
blotched-blue-tongue.size: Snout to base of tail up to 37 cm, with length also given as 35–50 cm and 550 mm. Weight is given as 300–500 g, and some individuals may weigh more than 1 kg.
blotched-blue-tongue.habitat: Open country with tussocky grasses or leaf litter, wet and dry sclerophyll forest, woodland, montane woodland, coastal heath, grassland, gardens and built-up areas. It shelters at night under leaf litter, rocks and logs, basks in the morning, and has a home range of 0.5–2 ha.
blotched-blue-tongue.diet: It eats plants and animals, mostly slow-moving prey, and its jaws crush snail shells and beetles. Food includes insects, snails, slugs, grasshoppers, beetles, carrion, fungi, fruit, berries, flowers and wildflowers; a local meal is not well documented.
blotched-blue-tongue.activeSeason: Active by day, inactive in cold weather, and may bask on sunny days. Local sightings are only from October 2021 and September 2024, so a local season is not well documented.
blotched-blue-tongue.breeding: Females give birth three to five months after spring mating, from December to April, with up to 25 young dispersing within a few days. Males mature over 1 year and females over 2; they live 12–15 years, and a local birth is not well documented.
blotched-blue-tongue.hangouts: A 31 October 2021 sighting is placed at Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve, but about 2,510 m accuracy is too coarse for a log, track or picnic area. A 20 September 2024 sighting, accuracy 4 m, is in Teesdale VIC 3328, with no street named.
blotched-blue-tongue.threats: Mowing long grass, warm roads, snail bait, dogs and cats are hazards, with no local roadkill, cat attack or bait case recorded. It has no venom and may or may not bite if picked up; ring Wildlife Victoria (03) 8400 7300 or DEECA 136 186.
blotched-blue-tongue.conservation: It is not on the FFG Threatened List and has no EPBC threatened-species row. Wildlife Act protection applies, and the IUCN status is not well documented.

whites-skink.identification: White's Skink (Liopholis whitii) is grey-brown with a red-brown flush toward the tail. Some are unpatterned above; others have two black stripes with white or yellow spots, sides plain or mottled, a white to light grey belly and a pale streak under the eye.
whites-skink.habitat: They use rocky places with a well-developed canopy, basking and foraging on outcrops and sheltering in burrows under rock slabs or logs. Habitat includes rocky microhabitats in open woodland, dry forests and coastal heathlands; the Inverleigh record does not say the animals were on rock.
whites-skink.diet: They feed on invertebrates. Prey in the 1995 record is not well documented.
whites-skink.activeSeason: They are active during the day. The only local date is 22 August 1995.
whites-skink.breeding: Females give birth to live young rather than laying eggs, one to three offspring each brood. Two animals near Inverleigh were captured and released and are not described as a mother and young.
whites-skink.hangouts: No record is inside 5 km. On 22 August 1995 two animals were captured and released 7 km south of Inverleigh (about 6.18 km; uncertainty 100 m); no creek, road or reserve is named.
whites-skink.threats: No threat is written for the 1995 record. If disturbed they retreat quickly.
whites-skink.conservation: Liopholis whitii was not found on the FFG Threatened List or the EPBC list. It is protected under the Wildlife Act 1975; its IUCN status is not well documented.
whites-skink.size: Snout to base of tail is up to 11 cm.

striped-legless-lizard.identification: Striped Legless Lizard (Delma impar), also Many-lined Delma or Striped Snake-lizard, is a pale grey to grey-brown pygopodid with dark side stripes, a cream underside, ear openings and a fleshy undivided tongue. Hind limbs are small flaps beside the vent, with 13–16 mid-body scale rows.
striped-legless-lizard.size: Snout-vent length reaches 9 cm or about 12 cm. Overall length is up to 30 cm, and the tail is longer than the body.
striped-legless-lizard.habitat: A grassland specialist of native grassland, nearby grassy woodland and exotic pasture on grassy basalt plains, often under logs, rocks and leaf litter. Communities include Natural Temperate Grassland and Grassy Eucalypt Woodland of the Victorian Volcanic Plain, and a stewardship region runs south to Inverleigh.
striped-legless-lizard.diet: It is a carnivore, feeding on insects and invertebrates. Prey around Inverleigh is not well documented.
striped-legless-lizard.activeSeason: It is noctidiurnal. When it is active around Inverleigh is not well documented.
striped-legless-lizard.breeding: It is egg-laying, can live more than 10 years and starts mating after 3–4 years. Clutch size and local nests are not well documented.
striped-legless-lizard.hangouts: None inside 10 km. Nearest named places are Boonderoo Nature Conservation Reserve near Teesdale (about 14.75–14.8 km), a coarse Winchelsea point (about 15.1 km) and Cressy-Shelford Road (about 17.6 km).
striped-legless-lizard.threats: No local injury tally is recorded, and any local decline from grassland loss is not well documented. Leave grassland cover, do not kill a striped legless animal as a snake, and do not pick one up if you are unsure what it is.
striped-legless-lizard.conservation: Vulnerable under the EPBC Act since 16 July 2000, and Endangered in Victoria under the Flora and Fauna Guarantee Act on the July 2026 list. Wildlife Act protection also applies.

eastern-snake-necked-turtle.identification: Chelodina longicollis is a long-necked turtle in the family Chelidae, also called the Snake-necked Turtle or Eastern Snake-necked Turtle. A shell and a long neck separate it from the skinks, dragon and legless lizard here; it is not a lizard or a snake.
eastern-snake-necked-turtle.habitat: Habitat is not well documented. Nearby records are two place guesses on the Teesdale side of the circle and one coordinate with no locality, and they are not a named wetland.
eastern-snake-necked-turtle.activeSeason: Nearby records are from November (2) and October (1), in 2020 and 2023. Three rows are not a season, so the active season is not well documented.
eastern-snake-necked-turtle.breeding: Breeding is not well documented. No local nest is described.
eastern-snake-necked-turtle.hangouts: Nothing inside 5 km. Two research grade records on 4 November 2020 are about 6.39 km and 6.41 km away, place guesses Teesdale-Inverleigh Road and Teesdale VIC 3328; one on 3 October 2023 about 9.31 km away has no locality and names no creek.
eastern-snake-necked-turtle.threats: No injury is written on these three rows, and the Teesdale-Inverleigh Road place guess is not a statement that the turtle was hit. It is protected under the Wildlife Act 1975; injured wildlife contacts are Wildlife Victoria (03) 8400 7300 and DEECA 136 186.
eastern-snake-necked-turtle.conservation: Chelodina longicollis was not found on the FFG Threatened List and was not returned in an EPBC search for this name. Wildlife Act 1975 protection still applies; its IUCN status is not well documented.

lizard-friendly-garden.identification: Accepted records inside 10 km are Jacky lizard, eastern three-lined skink, garden skink, eastern and blotched blue-tongues, plus White's skink in the outer ring. The striped legless lizard was not returned inside 10 km, and a small brown skink is not automatically a garden skink.
lizard-friendly-garden.habitat: Shelter is logs, rocks and leaf litter: blue-tongues use open country with tussocky grasses, garden skinks use rock piles and suburban gardens, and Jacky lizards bask on logs and fallen branches. The Inverleigh reserve's ground layer is wallaby grass, which is that reserve's vegetation.
lizard-friendly-garden.diet: Blue-tongues eat snails, slugs, insects and some plants, so snail bait reaches them. Garden skinks and the three-lined skink are invertebrate feeders, Jacky lizards take small arthropods, and never feed blue-tongues.
lizard-friendly-garden.activeSeason: Where recorded, dated lizards are diurnal. Blue-tongues are inactive in cold weather and may bask on sunny days; small-skink records include July, and record months are not a survey.
lizard-friendly-garden.breeding: Jacky lizards lay eggs; clutch size is not well documented. Three-lined skinks lay up to five eggs, sometimes with other females; garden skinks up to four in communal nests; blue-tongues and White's skink give birth to live young, litter size not well documented.
lizard-friendly-garden.hangouts: Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve, Inverleigh Conservation Reserve, Inverleigh Common, Old Teesdale Track, Old Shelford Track, Bannockburn, Bannockburn Bush, Harvey Road paddocks, Mason's Road (900 m uncertainty). Inverleigh VIC 3321, Teesdale VIC 3328, a Spring Creek Road blue-tongue roadkill, White's skink 7 km S of Inverleigh.
lizard-friendly-garden.threats: Snail bait poisons blue-tongues that eat poisoned snails or slugs; call (03) 8400 7300 or 13 11 26. Blue-tongues hide in long grass; Spring Creek Road roadkill 25 May 2017; local bait death is not well documented, and dog or cat attacks can be fatal.
lizard-friendly-garden.conservation: Those six species are not on the July 2026 FFG Threatened List or the 28 August 2026 EPBC extract. Every native reptile is protected under Wildlife Act 1975; northern blue-tongue subspecies is EPBC Critically Endangered, not marked for Victoria; Golden Plains page not well documented.

legless-vs-snake.identification: Legless lizards, related to geckos, are not snakes. External ear, scaly flaps beside the cloaca, undivided tongue and a tail usually at least as long as the snout-vent length mark them—do not pick one up; no Hooded Scaly-foot or Patternless Delma within 50 km.
legless-vs-snake.habitat: No legless-lizard habitat was recorded inside 10 km. The Corangamite CMA stewardship region names the striped legless lizard and includes Inverleigh as its southern edge, which is not a sighting.
legless-vs-snake.diet: A separate diet is not well documented. Insects are listed for the striped legless lizard.
legless-vs-snake.activeSeason: Delma impar is noctidiurnal. Local months are not well documented.
legless-vs-snake.breeding: Delma impar is oviparous. Clutch size is not well documented; breeding method is not a safe field test, since local snakes include live-bearing elapids.
legless-vs-snake.hangouts: No legless-lizard hangout inside 10 km. The nearest named striped legless lizard place is Boonderoo Nature Conservation Reserve at Teesdale, about 14.8 km, with coarser points further out; these are not Inverleigh.
legless-vs-snake.threats: Do not kill it as a snake or pick up a small snake. If bitten and it might be a snake, use snake-bite first aid and call triple zero (000); killing or taking one without a permit is an offence under the Wildlife Act 1975.
legless-vs-snake.conservation: The only pygopodid in the wider search was Delma impar (EPBC Vulnerable, FFG Endangered), and it was not inside 10 km. Other listed legless lizards, including Aprasia parapulchella and Aprasia aurita, had no genus records within 50 km.
